name: Contrived Benchmarks
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: When the Test Is Rigged to Be Winnable
lesson.summary: Many headline quantum computing results come from benchmarks specifically engineered to be hard for classical computers and easy for quantum ones, which makes them poor evidence of real world usefulness.
lesson.body:
Put the last two chapters together and a pattern becomes clear. Quantum supremacy asks only whether a quantum computer beat the best classical method at some task, with no requirement that the task be useful. Quantum advantage raises the bar to problems people actually care about, and, as covered, that higher bar has rarely if ever been cleanly and durably cleared. The gap between those two standards is filled, in practice, by a category of tasks worth naming directly: contrived benchmarks, problems chosen specifically because they are difficult for classical computers and comparatively easy for quantum ones, with little to no connection to any application anyone would otherwise want solved.

Random circuit sampling, the task behind Google's 2019 Sycamore claim, is the clearest example. The circuit being sampled was not selected because its output was valuable, it was selected because a quantum processor can physically run it easily while classical simulation of the same circuit scales very badly. Boson sampling, the photonic equivalent used in experiments like the Jiuzhang series, works the same way: sample from the output distribution of photons passing through a random network of optical elements, a distribution believed to be classically hard to compute but with no known independent use once you have it. These tasks are sometimes described, fairly, as designed for the quantum computer to win rather than designed around a problem that needed solving in the first place.

This is not necessarily dishonest science. Demonstrating that a physical device can reliably execute and measure a computation believed to be classically intractable is a legitimate and difficult engineering achievement, and it does provide real evidence about the maturity of a platform's control, calibration, and error rates. The trouble comes from how these results get communicated afterward, when a benchmark engineered to showcase a narrow quantum strength gets described in press coverage as though it demonstrates broad, practical quantum superiority over classical computing in general, a much larger and unsupported claim.

A useful habit for evaluating any quantum computing headline is to ask two questions the benchmark itself will not answer for you: was this task chosen because it matters, or because it was winnable, and has anyone shown that improved classical algorithms cannot close the gap later, the way they did after the original Sycamore claim and after several subsequent supremacy style results. Quantum volume and other single number benchmarks face a related criticism: they compress a genuinely multidimensional comparison, the same one covered back in the platform comparison chapter, spanning qubit count, coherence, gate fidelity, and connectivity, into one figure that is easy to put in a press release and much harder to interpret honestly. None of this means quantum computing has made no progress. It means that distinguishing a real, durable, useful speedup from a benchmark built to be won is the single most important skill for reading quantum computing news critically, and it is exactly the skill this chapter and the two before it were built to give you.
